name: Tomb of Tutankhamun
info: The tomb of Tutankhamun, KV62, is a small burial place in the Valley of the Kings, adapted for a pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty who died young and found in 1922 with 5,398 objects of his burial goods.

facts.made: Commissioned for Tutankhamun, an Eighteenth Dynasty pharaoh who reigned c. 1332–1323 BCE; probably begun as a non-royal tomb, possibly intended for his advisor Ay, and enlarged after the king's premature death
facts.form: A rock-cut tomb of four chambers (antechamber, annexe, burial chamber and treasury) with an entrance staircase of sixteen steps and a corridor 8 metres long; painted decoration only in the burial chamber
facts.where: In the eastern branch of the Valley of the Kings, cut into the valley floor; the mummy and sarcophagus remain in the tomb, most of the goods were sent to Cairo and have been moving to the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza
facts.known: a complete set of royal burial goods; the golden funerary mask; the gilded shrines and nested coffins; the discovery of 1922 by Howard Carter; the media frenzy called Tutmania; the rumoured curse; evidence of ancient tomb robbery

t: KV62 is smaller and less decorated than other royal tombs of its time and probably began as a tomb for a non-royal person, so its 5,398 objects had to be packed densely into the space.
Robbers entered twice within a few years of the burial, but the tomb was resealed and then buried under debris, so Tutankhamun's mummy and most of the goods stayed intact.
Howard Carter and Lord Carnarvon found it in 1922; the clearance took ten digging seasons, and most of the contents went to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo rather than being divided with the sponsors.
dyk: Among the furniture was a foldable bed, the only intact example known from ancient Egypt, and a reed staff labelled as one that the king "cut with his own hand".
ev: Tutankhamun was buried in KV62, which was robbed twice within a few years and resealed each time
Howard Carter's excavators found the first step of the entrance staircase and reached the antechamber on 26 November
The excavators opened the coffins and removed the mummy, and a legal dispute with the Egyptian government over access ended
The last shipment of conserved burial goods was sent to Cairo
A theft from the sarcophagus after 1926 came to light when the anatomist Ronald Harrison re-examined the remains
A rainstorm flooded the tomb through a fault in the burial chamber ceiling
The mummy was moved to a climate-controlled glass display case in the antechamber
A renovation of the tomb, begun with the Getty Conservation Institute in 2009, was completed

sections.origins:
Tutankhamun reigned c. 1332–1323 BCE, towards the end of the Eighteenth Dynasty in the New Kingdom. He took the throne as a child after the death of Akhenaten, who was probably his father, and the brief reigns of Neferneferuaten and Smenkhkare. Akhenaten had reshaped Egyptian religion by worshipping a single deity, Aten, and rejecting the others. Tutankhamun restored traditional practice and changed his name from Tutankhaten to Tutankhamun, honouring Amun.

Soon after he took power he commissioned a full-size royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings, probably one of two tombs, WV23 or KV57. KV62 is thought to have been a non-royal tomb, possibly intended for his advisor Ay, and it was enlarged for the king's burial after his premature death. Ay became pharaoh and was buried in WV23. Because Ay was elderly, it is possible that he buried his predecessor in KV62 so as to take WV23 for himself. Ay was succeeded by the general Horemheb, who tried to erase Akhenaten and his successors from the record.
sections.content:
The tomb lies in the eastern branch of the valley, cut into limestone bedrock in the valley floor and running beneath a low foothill. Its design resembles non-royal tombs of its time, elabourated to follow the plan of a royal tomb. A stairway descends to a corridor, then to an antechamber, with an annexe at its southwest corner, a burial chamber to the north and a treasury east of the burial chamber. The burial chamber and treasury may have been added when the tomb was adapted for Tutankhamun.

Only the burial chamber is decorated, painted with figures on a yellow background; none of the decoration is in relief. The north wall shows Ay performing the Opening of the Mouth ritual on the mummy, and Tutankhamun greeting Nut and Osiris. The east wall shows the funeral procession, an image common in private New Kingdom tombs but found in no other royal tomb. The west wall bears twelve baboons from the Amduat, a funerary text about the sun god Ra's journey through the netherworld. The goods number 5,398 objects, including 413 shabtis, figurines meant to do work for the king in the afterlife, and more than 200 pieces of jewellery.
sections.making:
The stairway originally had sixteen steps. The lowest six were cut away during the burial to make room to manoeuvre the largest pieces of funerary furniture through the doorway, then rebuilt, then removed again 3,400 years later when the excavators took out the same furniture. The corridor is 8 metres long and 1.7 metres wide, and the antechamber measures 7.9 by 3.6 metres. The burial chamber is 4 by 6.4 metres, and each of its walls has a niche holding a "magic brick" inscribed with Spell 151 of the Book of the Dead to ward off threats to the deceased.

Most of the burial chamber was taken up by a gilded wooden outer shrine, enclosing a linen pall, three nested inner shrines and a stone sarcophagus with three nested coffins. The sarcophagus is quartzite with a red granite lid painted yellow to match, carved with four protective goddesses. The outer two coffins are gilded wood inlaid with glass and semiprecious stones, while the innermost was primarily 110.4 kilograms of solid gold. The shrines are decorated in relief with extracts from the Book of the Dead, the Amduat and the earliest known copy of the Book of the Heavenly Cow.
sections.reception:
The tomb's contents have been read as evidence for several questions. The Egyptologist Joyce Tyldesley argues that larger tombs may have held assemblages of similar size, arranged more spaciously. Parallels in other royal tombs imply a somewhat standard set of object types, and no papyri were found, to the disappointment of Egyptologists who hoped for documents on the Amarna Period. Its value lay instead in the material culture it preserved: clothing more varied than art of the time shows, and objects of the shift in religious policy, such as a golden throne whose names had been altered.

Wine jars labelled Year 5 to Year 9 of the reign suggest that Tutankhamun ruled for nine or ten years, and the garlands point to a funeral in mid-March to mid-April. The thefts make the tomb an important source on tomb robbery in the New Kingdom: dockets on the boxes show that about 60 percent of the jewellery boxes' contents is missing. In the 1920s the discovery produced a media frenzy dubbed "Tutmania" and a fashion for Egyptian design motifs in the West, while in Egypt it reinforced pharaonism, the ideology stressing the country's link to its ancient past.
sections.survival:
Within a few years of the burial, robbers entered twice. After the first robbery officials repaired and repacked some goods and filled the corridor with limestone chips; a second set of robbers burrowed through the fill, and the tomb was resealed after a second hasty restoration. Flash floods left alluvium over the valley, and more than 150 years later the cutting of KV9 added debris and workers' huts over the entrance. When the valley's tombs were stripped in the late Twentieth and Twenty-first Dynasties, Tutankhamun's tomb, buried and forgotten, remained undisturbed.

Theodore M. Davis's excavators never found it, because he thought no tomb would be cut into the valley floor. The discovery began on 4 November 1922. Conserving the contents took ten digging seasons, and Carter, the chemist Alfred Lucas and the photographer Harry Burton worked throughout. After a dispute that ended in January 1925, the goods were not divided between the government and the sponsors but mostly went to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. Carter took a handful of small artefacts without permission, which his heir returned. Since the discovery water has trickled in and the 1991 flood stained a wall; a replica of the burial chamber by Factum Arte opened in 2014.
sections.legacy:
The find brought Tutankhamun wide fame under the nickname "King Tut", and artefacts such as the golden funerary mask are among the best-known artworks from ancient Egypt. Lord Carnarvon's death from an infection in April 1923 inspired rumours of a curse on the tomb, and other deaths and strange events came to be attributed to it. Selected pieces have toured Europe, North America, Japan and Australia in three phases, from 1961 to 1967, 1972 to 1981 and 2004 to 2013, raising money for the Egyptian government.

Study of the remains has been contentious. In 1996 Bob Brier suggested that bone fragments in the skull were a sign of a blow to the head, but they were later found to be vertebrae pushed in during Derry's examination. A 2010 genetic study named Tutankhamun as the father of two foetuses found in the treasury, though geneticists such as Svante Pääbo question results from Egyptian mummies. In 2015 Nicholas Reeves argued from scans that hidden chambers lay behind the burial chamber walls; radar examinations in 2016 and 2018 found no voids, while a 2026 study claims they are still possible.

summary: KV62, in the Valley of the Kings, was probably begun as a non-royal tomb and enlarged for Tutankhamun after his early death. Robbed twice and then buried under debris, it was found intact in 1922 by Howard Carter, and its 5,398 objects went mostly to Cairo.

notes: The article gives two reign dates for Tutankhamun: c. 1332–1323 BC in the lead and c. 1334–1325 BC in the History section. The text uses the lead's; start -1332 with circa true is that figure, the tomb's making being undated.
The tomb's own building date is not given; the key event 14th century BCE covers the burial, taken from the reign dates.
Reeves's 2015 chambers claim, the 2016/2018 radar results and the 2026 microgravity study are as the article states them.
The article says Davis's KV54 objects and KV58 chariot harness pieces, the Hittite 'Dakhamunzu' letter's date mismatch and the Stephen Cross / Andreas Dorn flood dispute; left out for length.
The article's Further reading holds works with no full bibliography; references are left empty for the editor.
The 1925 event pairs the mummy's removal with the end of the legal dispute (January 1925); the mummy examination is dated November 1925 in the article.
